stem: What does a Prometheus client library do inside your application?

options.text: Pushes metrics to Prometheus every few seconds
options.note: Client libraries expose metrics for pulling by default.

options.text: Evaluates alerting rules inside the application
Defines metrics and serves them over HTTP
Stores metrics in a local time series database

explanation: Client libraries let you define and expose internal metrics via an HTTP endpoint on your application's instance, serving current state when scraped.

stem: Your team writes its services in Rust and wants an officially maintained Prometheus client library. What's the situation?

options.note: Prometheus maintains its own Rust library.

options.text: Only the Go and Java libraries are official
options.note: Python, Ruby, Rust and Node.js are official too.

options.text: There's an official Rust client library
options.note: Right. client_rust is listed as official.

options.text: Rust services need an exporter instead
options.note: Exporters are for code you can't instrument directly.

explanation: Official client libraries are listed for Go, Java or Scala, Node.js, Python, Ruby and Rust; many other languages have third-party libraries.

stem: A counter with no labels is created at startup but nothing has happened yet. What do most client libraries expose?

options.note: Unlabelled metrics are exported at 0 by most libraries.

options.text: The metric, with no value line
options.note: A sample line always has a value.

explanation: Most client libraries (including Go, Java and Python) automatically export a 0 for metrics with no labels.

stem: A counter has a `result` label with values success and failure. Failures are rare. What should you do so alerts on failures work reliably?

options.text: Add a timestamp label to each failure series
Create the failure series on the first failure
options.note: Then rate() and ratios break until it appears.

options.text: Use a gauge set to 1 while failures happen
options.note: Doesn't solve the missing-series problem, and loses counts.

options.text: Initialise both label values to 0 at startup
options.note: Right. Missing series are hard to query.

explanation: Avoid missing metrics: export a default value such as 0 for any time series you know may exist in advance.

stem: Many client libraries expose some metrics without you writing code. Which is a typical example?

options.note: Also generated by Prometheus at scrape time.
Request metrics depend on your instrumentation or framework.
up is generated by Prometheus at scrape time.

explanation: Client libraries typically offer standard process metrics such as process_cpu_seconds_total and process_start_time_seconds.

stem: In a client library, how do you record the duration of a request in a histogram?

options.text: Set the _sum gauge to the duration
Call inc() on the matching bucket
options.note: The library updates the cumulative buckets for you.

options.text: Push the duration to the Pushgateway

explanation: Histograms sample observations: the library updates bucket counts, _sum and _count when you observe a value.

stem: A client library supports exemplars. What is a typical use?

options.text: Attaching a trace ID to an observation
options.note: Right. It links metrics to traces.

options.text: Adding a user ID label to every series
Setting a retention period per series

explanation: Exemplars are references to data outside the metric set, commonly a trace ID, exposed in the OpenMetrics format.

stem: For an online-serving system, which metrics are key according to the docs?

options.note: Useful but not the key online-serving metrics.
Resource metrics alone miss what users experience.

explanation: The key metrics for online-serving systems are the number of performed queries, errors, and latency.

stem: A nightly report job sometimes silently stops running. Which metric lets you alert on that reliably?

options.text: A gauge with the Unix time of its last success
options.note: Right. Alert when time() minus it gets too large.

options.text: A gauge of how long the last run took
options.note: Useful, but it doesn't change when the job stops running.

options.text: A summary of rows processed in each run
options.note: This also goes quiet rather than alerting when runs stop.

options.text: A counter of failed runs, alerting on increases
options.note: If the job stops running, nothing fails, so this never fires.

explanation: The key metric of a batch job is the last time it succeeded. Alert when it hasn't succeeded recently enough.

stem: What's the general guideline for label cardinality on most metrics?

options.note: Right. Investigate anything over 100 or likely to grow.
Every label combination is a series.

explanation: Try to keep the cardinality of your metrics below 10, and for metrics exceeding that, aim to limit them to a handful across your whole system.

stem: To track when something last happened, what should a metric expose?

options.text: Seconds since it happened, kept updated
options.note: That needs constant updating and breaks if the app stops.

options.text: The Unix timestamp of the event
options.note: Right. time() - metric gives the age.

options.text: A log line written when it happens
A counter that increments every second

explanation: Timestamps, not time since: export the Unix timestamp at which something happened, and calculate time since in PromQL.

stem: In an offline processing pipeline, what do the docs suggest to see how long items take to pass through?

options.text: A summary per item with an item_id label
Polling the database row count per stage
Graphing irate() of the queue size
options.note: That's not how the docs suggest it.

options.text: A timestamped heartbeat through each stage

explanation: For offline processing, send a heartbeat through the system that includes the timestamp; each stage exports the most recent heartbeat timestamp it saw.

stem: How should you instrument failures alongside total requests?

options.text: Log the failures and skip metrics
options.note: Metrics are needed for alerting on rates.

options.text: A failure counter plus a total counter
A failure counter with no total
options.note: You need the total for a ratio.

options.text: A gauge that's set to 1 while failing

explanation: Every time there is a failure, increment a counter. When reporting failures you should generally also have a metric for the total number of attempts, so the failure ratio can be calculated.

stem: You know the latency target is 300 ms but need to aggregate across instances. What's the better instrumentation choice?

options.text: A summary with a 0.3 s objective
options.note: Summaries' quantiles still can't be aggregated across instances.
Summary quantiles can't be aggregated across instances.

options.text: A histogram with a bucket at 0.3 s
options.note: Right. Aggregatable, and accurate at the threshold.

options.text: A gauge of the last request's latency

explanation: Use histograms if you need to aggregate; place a bucket at a known threshold for an accurate fraction.

stem: Which is the best name for a counter of processed jobs?

options.note: _count is used by histograms and summaries.

explanation: An accumulating count has total as a suffix, in addition to the unit if applicable.

stem: A latency metric is measured in milliseconds in your code. What should it be named and exposed as?

options.note: The unit should be in the name, and in seconds.
Not base units; _total is only for counters.

explanation: Metrics should use base units (seconds, bytes, meters) and include the unit in the name, e.g. http_request_duration_seconds.

stem: How should a metric for disk usage as a proportion be exposed?

options.note: ratio means 0–1; a 0–100 value under that name misleads.
The docs prefer ratios from 0 to 1.

explanation: Percent is expressed as a ratio with values 0–1 rather than 0–100; ratio is used as a suffix, e.g. disk_usage_ratio.

stem: What should the first part of a metric name be?

options.text: The version of the instrumenting library
options.note: Versions belong in an info metric's labels.

options.text: The hostname of the exporting machine

explanation: Metric names should have a single-word application prefix relevant to the domain, sometimes called the namespace.

stem: Which naming approach follows best practice?

options.note: Don't encode label values in names.
_total is a suffix, not a label.

explanation: Use labels to differentiate the characteristics of the thing being measured, e.g. api_http_requests_total with operation="create|update|delete".

stem: Why is `request_size_and_duration` a bad metric?

options.note: The bigger problem is mixing two quantities.

explanation: A metric name must refer to a single unit and a single quantity; don't mix request size with request duration.

stem: How is build version information usually exposed?

options.note: Right. Constant value 1, data in labels.

options.text: A version label on every metric

explanation: Pseudo-metrics with an _info suffix carry information in labels and have a constant value of 1, e.g. foobar_build_info.

stem: When do you use an exporter?

options.text: When you can't instrument the code

options.note: Direct instrumentation is preferred when possible.

explanation: Exporters help export existing metrics from third-party systems as Prometheus metrics, when instrumenting directly isn't feasible.

stem: You need disk, CPU and memory metrics for 200 Linux VMs. What's the usual approach?

options.text: Run the Node exporter on each VM
options.note: Right. One per machine, scraped by Prometheus.

options.text: One Blackbox exporter probing all VMs
options.note: Blackbox probes endpoints; it can't see inside hosts.

options.text: Add a client library to each VM's kernel
options.note: Client libraries instrument your own code.

options.text: Push from each VM to a Pushgateway

explanation: The node exporter exposes hardware- and kernel-related metrics; exporters run beside what they monitor.

stem: You need to check that a public HTTPS endpoint responds and its certificate is valid, from the outside. Which exporter fits?

options.note: That reads files on a host.
Right. It probes endpoints over HTTP, DNS, TCP and ICMP.

explanation: The blackbox exporter probes endpoints such as HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, TCP and ICMP; Prometheus passes it the target to probe.

stem: How do the docs recommend deploying an exporter like haproxy_exporter?

options.text: One central exporter for all HAProxies

explanation: Each exporter should monitor exactly one instance application, preferably beside it; all service discovery is done in Prometheus.

stem: Should an exporter set timestamps on the metrics it exposes?
explanation: You should not set timestamps on the metrics you expose; let Prometheus take care of that.

stem: When should an exporter fetch data from the application it monitors?

options.text: Only when an alert is firing
On its own timer every few seconds
options.note: The docs prefer fetching on scrape.

explanation: Metrics should be pulled from the application only when Prometheus scrapes, using custom collectors that build metrics fresh on each scrape.

stem: An exporter can reach its host but not the database it monitors. What's a common way to signal that?

options.note: Right. Prometheus's up only shows the exporter was scraped.
up is generated by Prometheus; an exporter shouldn't expose it.

options.text: Serve an empty page with HTTP 200
options.note: That hides the failure; the docs suggest a 5xx error or an _up metric.

explanation: When an exporter can't reach its application, the docs give two options: return a 5xx error, or expose a myexporter_up metric (e.g. haproxy_up) of 0 or 1. The latter is better when some useful metrics are still available.
